summary.text: Petrified wood is fossilized wood from land plants in which the tree's material has been replaced by stone through mineralization.
It forms when wood is buried in wet sediment or volcanic ash, where a lack of oxygen slows decay and dissolved minerals fill and replace the cells.
Unlike most plant fossils, which are impressions or compressions, it keeps the wood's three-dimensional form, often with cell walls in great detail.

facts.label: Main mineral
facts.value: Silica, as opal, chalcedony or quartz

facts.label: Fastest formation
facts.value: Within hundreds of years in silica-rich hot springs

items.prompt: One log is quickly buried in wet mud, while another lies on a dry forest floor. Why is the buried log far more likely to become petrified?

options.label: The mud's weight presses the wood into rock
Being sealed off from oxygen slows its decay
Wet wood is too soft for insects to eat
The warm mud bakes the wood until it hardens

items.explain: Burial in water-soaked sediment cuts off oxygen, which the bacteria and fungi that rot wood need, giving minerals time to replace it.

items.prompt: If you analysed a chunk of petrified wood, what would make up most of it?

options.label: The original wood fibers
Iron and other metals
Silica, the stuff of quartz
Calcite, the mineral of chalk

items.explain: Only around 10% of the original material remains, and the rest is nearly pure silica.

items.prompt: A fossil hunter finds a fossil leaf print and a log of petrified wood. What usually sets the log apart?

options.label: It keeps the plant's full three-dimensional shape
It is still made mostly of the original wood
It formed out in the open air above ground
It shows only a flat outline pressed into rock

items.explain: Most plant fossils are impressions or compressions, but petrified wood is a three-dimensional copy of the original material.

items.prompt: Turning wood to stone normally takes a very long time. Where can it happen within just hundreds of years?

options.label: On the floor of a deep ocean trench
Under the sand of desert dunes
In permanently frozen arctic soil
In hot springs rich in silica

items.explain: Silica-rich hot springs can coat and soak into wood quickly, petrifying it within hundreds of years.

items.prompt: Petrified logs formed underground are often found lying out in the open today. How did they usually get there?

options.label: Volcanic eruptions threw them onto the surface
Erosion wore away the sediment around them
Floods carried them up out of the ground
Earthquakes split the ground and lifted them

items.explain: Petrified wood is later exposed when the surrounding sediments are eroded away.

items.prompt: Erosion uncovers two buried logs: one petrified, one that never mineralized. What happens next?

options.label: Both crumble away at about the same rate
The petrified log soon dissolves in rain
The other log is quickly destroyed
The other log slowly hardens to stone

items.explain: Fossil wood that has not mineralized is rapidly destroyed once exposed, while petrified wood is quite durable.
